title: Using Ray Direct Transport for Fast and Easy Weight Syncing in Reinforcement Learning (Part 2) | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale details Ray Direct Transport (RDT), a Ray Core layer that piggybacks RDMA metadata onto Ray's data-transfer protocol to make RDMA-backed weight syncing in LLM reinforcement learning both fast and easy. Using RDT best practices (pre-registered memory, direct-to-target writes, and a memory pool) improves on a naive RDMA implementation by up to 7.5x on GB200 nodes, and integrations with RL frameworks SkyRL and Miles cut weight-sync times by 2.2x-18x over NCCL/Mooncake baselines.

insights.claim: Ray Direct Transport (RDT) is a Ray Core feature that provides native RDMA-based transfers between Ray actors, acting as a glue layer between Ray-based engines like vLLM and third-party RDMA libraries such as NVIDIA's NIXL.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: RDT is Anyscale's play to own the developer-facing abstraction for high-performance weight syncing, keeping vLLM/NIXL adopters inside the Ray ecosystem.
insights.quote: RDT acts as an intermediate “glue” layer between open-source engines built on Ray such as vLLM and third-party libraries such as NIXL that provide RDMA-based device-to-device transfers.
insights.locator: In Part 1, we introduced Ray Direct Transport

insights.claim: RDMA delivers high bandwidth via kernel bypass and zero-copy transfers, but requires the developer to manage memory allocation, memory registration, and metadata exchange, and naive implementations of these steps can eliminate any speedup from the transfer itself.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: The value of tooling like RDT is precisely in hiding this overhead; the moat in AI infra is increasingly in the orchestration glue, not the raw transport.
insights.quote: Naive implementations for these steps can easily eliminate any speedups in the data transfer itself.
insights.locator: Everyone knows that RDMA is fast

insights.claim: Ray's advantage as a distributed orchestrator is that it already has visibility into when and where data transfers need to happen, so RDT can piggyback only the necessary RDMA metadata onto Ray's existing data-transfer protocol while preserving Ray's developer-friendly APIs.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Anyscale is arguing that owning the orchestrator is a structural edge for transport performance, a defensibility claim for Ray versus standalone RDMA libraries.
insights.quote: If we can piggy-back only the necessary RDMA metadata onto the existing Ray data transfer protocol, we can preserve Ray’s developer-friendly APIs but also benefit from RDMA-backed data transfer.
insights.locator: How do we resolve this tension in Ray?

insights.claim: Applying RDT best practices improved on a naive RDMA weight-syncing implementation by up to 7.5x on GB200 nodes using Multi-Node NVLink (MNNVL).
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Quantifies the payoff of the software layer on NVIDIA's newest hardware, a signal that GB200/NVLink deployments still leave large performance on the table without optimized transport.
insights.quote: we’ll show how to improve upon a naive RDMA implementation by up to 7.5x on GB200 nodes using Multi-Node NVLink (MNNVL).
insights.locator: In this Part 2, we’ll cover the best practices

insights.claim: On inter-node transfers between 2 GB200 nodes over MNNVL with 900 GB/s unidirectional point-to-point bandwidth, RDT achieved 859 GB/s for the data transfer itself.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Achieving ~95% of hardware peak bandwidth is a concrete efficiency proof point for evaluating RDT against raw RDMA stacks.
insights.quote: the max hardware transfer bandwidth is 900GB/s and we achieved 859 GB/s for the data transfer itself.
insights.locator: Data transfer: The actual transfer of tensor data

insights.claim: Untuned RDT weight syncing suffered performance bottlenecks that reduced actual transfer bandwidth from the hardware optimum by 10x or more before the team's fixes.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: The gap between naive and tuned RDMA is an order of magnitude, underscoring that hardware spend alone does not deliver performance in RL training clusters.
insights.quote: we found and fixed a number of performance bottlenecks that greatly reduce the actual transfer bandwidth from the hardware optimal, in some cases by 10x or more!
insights.locator: During testing of weights syncing with RDT

themes.theme: RDMA optimization techniques exposed as APIs

insights.claim: A single RDMA memory registration call can take tens of microseconds, which becomes a dominant overhead when a network can complete a 1GB transfer in milliseconds and each transfer contains many memory regions.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Memory registration, not the wire, is the hidden cost center in fast RDMA fabrics, guiding where infra teams should optimize.
insights.quote: one memory registration call can take 10s of us – it may not sound like much, but when your network is fast enough to complete a 1GB data transfer in milliseconds and each transfer contains many memory regions, the overhead can quickly add up.
insights.locator: However, these extra steps can also be a bit of a gotcha

insights.claim: RDT exposes ray.experimental.register_nixl_memory to pre-register the same tensors ahead of time, paying the registration cost once at actor creation rather than repeatedly during each transfer when source and destination buffers don't change.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: A concrete lever for RL weight-sync latency; teams evaluating transport stacks should check whether re-registration is amortized.

insights.claim: RDT's NIXL backend registers the base tensor only once and sends each subtensor as an offset into that base, avoiding the raw-NIXL practice of registering every subtensor separately when training and inference models are sharded differently.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Tensor-parallel resharding between trainer and inference engine is a common source of many-small-tensor overhead; this optimization directly targets it.
insights.quote: RDT’s NIXL backend implements an optimization where it only registers the base tensor once, then sends each subtensor as an offset into that base tensor.
insights.locator: Another case where memory registration can become expensive

insights.claim: The new ray.experimental.set_target_for_ref API lets RDT write incoming weights directly into the inference worker's model tensors, cutting peak GPU memory from 40GB to 20GB for a 20GB weight transfer by eliminating the extra staging-buffer copy.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Halving peak memory on the receiver frees GPU headroom in memory-constrained training/inference fleets, a direct cost lever.
insights.quote: Prior, we consistently saw an extra copy in the torch caching allocator, so with 20GB of weights you would see the peak be 40GB. Now, the peak remains at 20GB.

insights.claim: RDT provides a preregistered memory pool (register_nixl_memory_pool) that buckets many small tensors into a contiguous buffer to maximize network bandwidth, with additional memory-pool improvements slated for general availability in Ray 2.59.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Transferring many small tensors is slower than one big tensor even at equal bytes, so bucketing is a portable optimization pattern worth watching land in Ray 2.59.
insights.quote: Transferring many small tensors is slower than sending one big tensor, even if the total bytes transferred is the same.

insights.claim: RDT sends PyTorch tensor data over RDMA via NIXL while serializing the surrounding Python object over Ray's CPU dataplane, and for serialized payloads exceeding 100KB (such as a list of 10k tensors) Ray Core incurs an extra serialization/deserialization through its shared-memory store.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: The Python-object path is a residual bottleneck for large tensor lists; a diligence flag when benchmarking many-tensor RL workloads.
insights.locator: Python object transfer: RDT supports sending PyTorch tensors

insights.claim: Managing N tensors adds O(N) system operations such as shape tracking and destination-buffer verification, adding a few milliseconds to the total transfer time for the 10,000-view case.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Per-tensor metadata cost is the next optimization frontier RDT is targeting; relevant for heavily sharded models.

themes.theme: RL framework integrations and competitive baselines

insights.claim: With the RDT integration, SkyRL can sync weights for Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B across 4 8xH100 nodes in 3.5 seconds, about 18x faster than SkyRL's simple NCCL broadcast-based implementation.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: An 18x weight-sync speedup materially raises RL training throughput on large models; a concrete adoption driver for Ray in the RL stack.
insights.quote: SkyRL can sync weights for Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B across 4 8xH100 nodes in just 3.5s, about 18x faster than the simple NCCL broadcast-based implementation in SkyRL.

insights.claim: With RDT, the Miles framework can sync GLM-4.5-Air across four 8xH100 nodes in 2.3 seconds, 2.2x faster than using NCCL and 1.14x faster than using the Mooncake Transfer Engine.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: RDT beats both NCCL and Mooncake on the same hardware, positioning it competitively against the leading transfer engines in RL infra.
insights.quote: Miles is able to sync GLM-4.5-Air across four 8xH100 nodes in only 2.3s, 2.2x faster than using NCCL and 1.14x faster than using the Mooncake Transfer Engine.
insights.locator: An integration with Miles is also in progress

insights.claim: The RDT weight-syncing speedups will be made generally available through ongoing open-source integrations with RL frameworks like SkyRL and Miles.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Wang
insights.so_what: Distribution via open-source RL frameworks is Anyscale's path to embedding RDT as the default transport, worth tracking for ecosystem lock-in.
insights.quote: These speedups will be generally available through ongoing open-source integrations with RL frameworks like SkyRL and Miles.
